title: Abba Joseph's ten lamps
hookLine: Abba Joseph lifts his hands, his fingers like ten lamps: why not become all flame?
carry: not a longer list: the whole self, given
tomorrow: a hunter finds Antony laughing with his monks. why?

cards: A habit tracker shows a perfect week. Every box checked, a little flame for the streak. And still the thought comes: what else should I add?
A monk named Lot carries that exact question across the desert to an older monk, Abba Joseph. As far as I can, he says, I keep my little round of prayers. I fast a little.
I pray, I think on scripture, I live at peace with others, and as far as I can, I keep my thoughts clean. So what else should I do? Joseph doesn't answer right away.

teach.b: He stretches his hands toward heaven, and the saying tells us his fingers became like ten lamps of fire. Then the answer: if you will, you can become all flame. That's the whole reply.
Look at what it does to Lot's list. Nothing on it is wrong, and Joseph throws none of it out.
But Lot measures in littles: as far as I can, a little. Joseph answers with all. Not more tasks.
The same prayers, the same peace, with the whole person caught up in them. And he answers with his body first.
The first letter to Timothy already pictures prayer that way: "I will therefore that men pray every where, lifting up holy hands, without wrath and doubting." Lot sees the answer before he hears it.
Here's the detail to tell a friend: the saying never says what Lot did next.
It stops on the offer. If you will. Nobody is pushed into the fire.
Like yesterday's leaking basket, the elder teaches with an action, not an argument.

how: Some Christians pray with hands raised or open, alone or in church, and this saying of Abba Joseph is one that people in the monastic tradition pass on.

o: a fire Joseph lit to warm the visiting monks
burning out from too many prayers and fasts
the whole life given to God, not a longer list

games.q: become all flame — tap the pairs.
p: as far as I can, a little

s: Abba Joseph tells Lot to drop his small prayers and fasts
he throws nothing out. he answers Lot's 'a little' with 'all'.
become all flame means piling on more religious tasks
the popular reading. Joseph adds no task at all; he lifts his hands.
the saying stops on the offer and never says what Lot did
if you will. it ends there, with the choice left open.

games.q: your friend volunteers at the food bank every Saturday, and spends most of the shift on her phone. by Abba Joseph's answer, what's missing?
o: more shifts, so it finally adds up to something.
nothing; showing up at all is the whole point.
not more hours: all of her, in the hours she gives.
games.why: Joseph didn't lengthen Lot's list or cut it. he answered 'a little' with 'all': the same shift, with the whole person in it.

practice: Sit up and turn your palms upward on your knees, or lift your hands a little if there's room. Keep them open for the whole sit, as if what you bring isn't a list but all of you.
If you pray, this is the posture the letter to Timothy describes.

wordCard.voice: Become all flame. Abba Joseph's answer to a monk who did everything a little: not one more task, the whole life set alight.

carryVoice: Your line: not a longer list: the whole self, given. Nothing on it thrown out, everything on it lit. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Apophthegmata Patrum), Joseph of Panephysis 7
